title: Happy Number
statement: Take a positive integer, square each of its digits and add the squares. Repeat with the result. If the process reaches 1 the number is happy. If it never does, it ends up circling through the same numbers forever. Say whether the starting number is happy.

example.caption: 19 becomes 82, then 68, then 100, then 1. It reaches 1, so it is happy.

idea.sentence: The sequence either reaches 1 or comes back to a number it has already seen, so keep a set of seen numbers and stop on either event.

jargon.plain: A run of numbers that repeats forever. Once a value shows up a second time, everything after it repeats too.
Split the number into its digits, square each one and add. For 82 that is 8² + 2² = 68.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a positive integer, like 19. Unhappy numbers make a loop of about 8 numbers, so keep it small.

vars.meaning: how many numbers appear before the chain hits 1 or repeats (small: under about 20 for any 32-bit input)

compare.bruteLabel: Keep a list, scan it for repeats each time
compare.optimalLabel: Set lookup, one check per number

rows.name: List of seen numbers
rows.note: Scan the whole list each step to see if the number is there.

rows.name: Set of seen numbers
rows.note: A lookup is O(1). Each step costs a digit split, about log n digits for the first number and 3 digits after that.

rows.name: Slow and fast pointers
rows.note: Floyd's cycle trick: one runner takes one step, one takes two. If they meet, there is a loop. No set needed.

fast.takeaway: After the first step the value is at most 810 for any 32-bit start, so k stays tiny. In practice both set and pointer versions are instant. The set is the simplest to read.

stages.title: Stop at 1 or a repeat
stages.note: The loop ends when the number is 1 (happy, return true) or when it is already in the set (a cycle, return false).

stages.title: Remember and step
stages.note: Put the number in the set, then replace it with the sum of its squared digits.

edges.title: The number 1
edges.why: It is already 1, so the loop never starts. 1 squared is 1, so it would stay there anyway.

edges.title: A number that falls into the 4-cycle
edges.why: 2 → 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4. Every unhappy number ends in this same loop, and the set notices the second 4.

edges.title: Trailing zeros
edges.why: 1 + 0 + 0 = 1 in one step. Zero digits add nothing, but they must not stop the digit loop early.

edges.title: Biggest 32-bit number
edges.why: Ten digits add up to a few hundred in one step. From there the chain is short, so a big input is no harder.

gotchas.text: n / 10 is a float division, not integer division. Use Math.floor(n / 10), or the loop never reaches 0 and the digits are wrong.
String(n).split('') hands you digit strings. d * d works only by coercion, and d + d would glue the text together. The n % 10 loop keeps every digit a number.
n / 10 on an int is integer division, so no floor is needed. A map[int]bool gives false for a missing key, so if seen[n] needs no second return value.
Do not loop 'a big fixed number of times' instead of tracking seen values. It happens to work, but it is a guess. The seen set proves a loop.

recap.pattern: Cycle detection on a number sequence
recap.key: Replace n by the sum of its squared digits. Stop at 1 (happy) or on a repeated number (loop, not happy).
recap.complexity: Time O(k log n). Space O(k), or O(1) with slow and fast pointers.
moves: If n is in the seen set, return false
Set n to its digit square sum
